title: jlbind
text:
Call Julia code from R without starting a Julia session.
jlbind compiles Julia code into a shared library with JuliaC.jl (by default with --trim=safe), and R calls it through R’s official C API. Thus, there is almost no overhead (see Performance).
Several R packages using jlbind can be installed side by side: their Julia code is compiled into one shared library.


# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("BjarkeHautop/jlbind")
Building the shared library requires Julia >= 1.13. Installing jlbind does not itself build the library.
Julia 1.14 or later is recommended: Julia 1.13 can compile a library that crashes as it loads when a function has a type parameter bounded by a Union (where {T<:Union{...}}), fixed in JuliaLang/julia#63664.



After installing or updating an R package that uses jlbind, build the shared library:
jlbind::install_library()
This compiles the Julia code of every installed package that uses jlbind and may take a few minutes. Run it again whenever you install or update one of them.
See Using packages built on jlbind for threads, troubleshooting and Julia dependency versions.



Set up a package with jlbind::use_jlbind(), then declare the Julia functions R can call in the generated binding package under inst/julia/:
module MyPkgBindings

using JLBind

greet(name::String) = "Hello, " * name * "!"
@rcall greet(name::String)::String

end
Run jlbind::update_entrypoints(), which generates the R function greet(name) that calls it.
See Get started with jlbind for a full walkthrough.



Contributions of all kinds are very welcome! You may use LLMs, but please write issue and PR descriptions in your own words. If you submit a PR, you should understand the code you’re contributing.

text: Source: R/runtime.R

title: Bind a package to the Julia library
text:
Description
Call this from the .onLoad() of a package that uses jlbind; use_jlbind() sets that up. The first call loads the compiled library, and each call binds one package’s routines to it. If the library is missing or was built from another version of the package, the package isn’t bound and its functions give an error; check_bound() says why.

title: Bind a package to the Julia library
text:
Usage
bind_client(pkg)

title: Bind a package to the Julia library
text:
Arguments



pkg


The package name.

title: Bind a package to the Julia library
text:
Details
The library is the one from install_library(), unless JLBIND_LIBRARY names another, or the first package bound was loaded with pkgload::load_all() and has one from build_library(). That library is rebuilt as the package loads if it is out of date with the package’s sources, as when its Julia code has changed. A library that has already loaded cannot be replaced, so after a change, restart R.
To run Julia with more threads, set JULIA_NUM_THREADS (a number or "auto") before loading the first package that uses jlbind.

title: Bind a package to the Julia library
text:
Value
Invisibly, TRUE if the package is bound and FALSE if not.

title: Update the list of Julia functions R can call
text: Source: R/scaffold.R

title: Update the list of Julia functions R can call
text:
Description
Finds the @rcall declarations in the package’s Julia binding package and generates the code that lets R call them. Run this whenever you add or remove an @rcall, or change its arguments. It writes two files:

title: Update the list of Julia functions R can call
text:
Usage
update_entrypoints(path = ".")

title: Update the list of Julia functions R can call
text:
Arguments



path


Path to the package sources.

title: Update the list of Julia functions R can call
text:
Details


src/entrypoints.h, from which src/jlbind.c registers a routine C_<name> for each declaration.


R/jlbind-wrappers.R, with an R function for each declaration that calls its routine. @rcall shift(x::Vector{Float64}, by::Float64 = 0.0)::Float64 becomes shift <- function(x, by = 0.0) .Call(C_shift, x, by).


Defaults must be literal numbers, strings, true, false or nothing (NULL). A function returning Nothing returns invisibly. To export or document a function, use a roxygen block on NULL with @name in another file. To add R code around a call, declare the Julia function with a jl_ prefix and write the R function yourself.

title: Update the list of Julia functions R can call
text:
Value
Invisibly, a data frame of the entrypoints with the columns name, nargs, and the formals, args and invisible (whether it returns invisibly) of their R wrappers.

title: Update the list of Julia functions R can call
text:
Examples

# A package set up with use_jlbind() in a temporary directory
pkg <- file.path(tempdir(), "addpkg")
dir.create(pkg)
writeLines(
  c(
    "Package: addpkg",
    "Title: Demo",
    "Version: 0.1.0",
    "Description: Demo.",
    "License: MIT"
  ),
  file.path(pkg, "DESCRIPTION")
)
use_jlbind(pkg)
#> Created the binding package addpkgBindings in /tmp/RtmpmTF1pS/addpkg/inst/julia.
#> Wrote /tmp/RtmpmTF1pS/addpkg/src/entrypoints.h (1 entrypoints).
#> Wrote /tmp/RtmpmTF1pS/addpkg/R/jlbind-wrappers.R.

# Add an entrypoint to the binding package, before its closing `end`
file <- file.path(pkg, "inst/julia/src/addpkgBindings.jl")
code <- readLines(file)
last <- max(which(code == "end"))
code <- append(
  code,
  c(
    "add(x::Float64, y::Float64) = x + y",
    "@rcall add(x::Float64, y::Float64)::Float64",
    ""
  ),
  after = last - 1L
)
writeLines(code, file)

update_entrypoints(pkg)
#> Wrote /tmp/RtmpmTF1pS/addpkg/src/entrypoints.h (2 entrypoints).
#> Wrote /tmp/RtmpmTF1pS/addpkg/R/jlbind-wrappers.R.
writeLines(readLines(file.path(pkg, "R", "jlbind-wrappers.R")))
#> # Generated by jlbind::update_entrypoints(): do not edit by hand
#> 
#> hello <- function(name) .Call(C_hello, name)
#> add <- function(x, y) .Call(C_add, x, y)

title: Set up a package to use jlbind
text:
Description
Adds what a package needs to call Julia code through jlbind.

title: Set up a package to use jlbind
text:
Usage
use_jlbind(path = ".", module = NULL, dir = "julia")

title: Set up a package to use jlbind
text:
Arguments



path


Path to the package sources.




module


Name of the Julia binding package. Defaults to the package name followed by Bindings. It must be unique across all packages that use jlbind, since they’re all compiled into one library.




dir


Directory under inst/ for the binding package.

title: Set up a package to use jlbind
text:
Details


A Julia binding package in inst/<dir>, with one example function, hello(). An existing binding package is left alone.


The C code that registers the package’s routines: src/jlbind.c and src/entrypoints.h (written by update_entrypoints()), and a rule in src/Makevars (created if needed) that recompiles jlbind.c when entrypoints.h changes.


R/jlbind.R, with an .onLoad() that calls bind_client(), and the roxygen tag for useDynLib(). If the package already has an .onLoad(), add jlbind::bind_client(pkgname) to it yourself.


The Config/jlbind and Imports: jlbind fields in DESCRIPTION.


.jlbind/, where build_library() writes a library for development, in .Rbuildignore and .gitignore.


R/jlbind-wrappers.R (written by update_entrypoints()), with an R function for each Julia function declared with @rcall.

title: Set up a package to use jlbind
text:
Value
path, invisibly.

title: Set up a package to use jlbind
text:
Examples

# A new package in a temporary directory
pkg <- file.path(tempdir(), "mypkg")
dir.create(pkg)
writeLines(
  c(
    "Package: mypkg",
    "Title: Demo",
    "Version: 0.1.0",
    "Description: Demo.",
    "License: MIT"
  ),
  file.path(pkg, "DESCRIPTION")
)

use_jlbind(pkg)
#> Created the binding package mypkgBindings in /tmp/Rtmpfz1Kby/mypkg/inst/julia.
#> Wrote /tmp/Rtmpfz1Kby/mypkg/src/entrypoints.h (1 entrypoints).
#> Wrote /tmp/Rtmpfz1Kby/mypkg/R/jlbind-wrappers.R.
list.files(pkg, recursive = TRUE)
#> [1] "DESCRIPTION"                     "inst/julia/Project.toml"        
#> [3] "inst/julia/src/mypkgBindings.jl" "NAMESPACE"                      
#> [5] "R/jlbind-wrappers.R"             "R/jlbind.R"                     
#> [7] "src/entrypoints.h"               "src/jlbind.c"                   
#> [9] "src/Makevars"

# The Julia binding package, with its example entrypoint
writeLines(readLines(file.path(pkg, "inst/julia/src/mypkgBindings.jl")))
#> """
#>     mypkgBindings
#> 
#> The R entrypoints of the R package mypkg. Each `@rcall` declaration
#> exports a Julia function to R; after changing them, run
#> `jlbind::update_entrypoints()` to regenerate the R functions that call them, in
#> `R/jlbind-wrappers.R`.
#> """
#> module mypkgBindings
#> 
#> using JLBind
#> 
#> hello(name::String) = "Hello, " * name * ", from Julia!"
#> 
#> @rcall hello(name::String)::String
#> 
#> end

Description
Deletes the library built by install_library(), with everything else jlbind stores in tools::R_user_dir("jlbind", "data"). Packages that use jlbind can’t call their Julia code until you run install_library() again.

remove_library()

title: Build a Julia library from specific packages
text: Source: R/library.R

title: Build a Julia library from specific packages
text:
Description
Like install_library(), but compiles only packages and writes the library to out, for package development. By default, it builds the package in the working directory into its .jlbind/ directory, which devtools::load_all() then uses instead of the library from install_library(). To use a library written elsewhere, set JLBIND_LIBRARY to its path before loading the package.

title: Build a Julia library from specific packages
text:
Usage
build_library(
  packages = ".",
  out = NULL,
  julia = NULL,
  versions = c("manifest", "compat"),
  develop = NULL
)

title: Build a Julia library from specific packages
text:
Arguments



packages


Paths to package sources or installed packages, or names of installed packages. An entry containing a / (or \ on Windows), or that is "." or "..", is a path; any other is a package name, so write "./mypkg" for the sources in the mypkg directory.




out


Directory to write the library to. Defaults to .jlbind/ in the sources of packages, which must then be a single path.




julia


Path to the julia executable. By default, the JULIA environment variable, or julia on the PATH.




versions


Where the Julia dependency versions come from. "manifest" keeps the versions in the first package’s Manifest.toml where the other packages’ [compat] bounds allow. "compat" ignores the manifests and lets Julia’s resolver choose versions from the [compat] bounds alone.




develop


Paths to local Julia packages to use instead of their released versions.

title: Build a Julia library from specific packages
text:
Value
The path to the library, invisibly.

title: Build a Julia library from specific packages
text:
Examples
# In the sources of a package that uses jlbind
build_library()
devtools::load_all()

# Several packages, used through JLBIND_LIBRARY
lib <- build_library(c("pkg1", "pkg2"), "jlbind-lib")
Sys.setenv(JLBIND_LIBRARY = lib)

title: Using packages built on jlbind
text:
Source: vignettes/using-clients.qmd
jlbind lets R packages call Julia code compiled ahead of time into a shared library, without a Julia session. This vignette explains how that library works and how to use an R package built with jlbind. To add Julia functions to your own R package, see Get started with jlbind. For how jlbind compares with other ways of calling Julia from R, see Performance.

title: Using packages built on jlbind
text:
How it works
An R process can load only one compiled Julia library. Julia has one runtime per process, and that runtime uses a single compiled image. If two R packages loaded separate copies of the library, they could conflict and crash the R session.
To avoid this, jlbind builds one shared library for each user, combining the Julia code of all installed R packages that use jlbind (clients). When you run install_library(), jlbind finds the installed clients, compiles their binding packages into one library, and saves it under tools::R_user_dir("jlbind", "data"). Loading a client loads that library and connects the client to it.
A client can only be bound to a library built from the version of that client currently installed. If you update a package without rebuilding the library, its functions will report that the library needs to be rebuilt.

title: Using packages built on jlbind
section: Using a package built on jlbind
text:
Using a package built on jlbind
You need Julia 1.13 or later to build the shared library.
After installing or updating an R package that uses jlbind, run:
jlbind::install_library()
The first build downloads and compiles the required Julia dependencies, so it may take a few minutes.






NoteRestart R after rebuilding a library that is already loaded



Julia cannot be restarted within an R session. If the old library has already been loaded, rebuilding it on disk does not replace the copy in memory. Restart R to use the new library.



If something doesn’t work correctly
If a package that uses jlbind doesn’t work, first check its status:
jlbind::check_bound("somepkg")
The most common causes are that the shared library hasn’t been built yet, or that the package was updated after the last build. For a full report, run:
jlbind::jlbind_sitrep()
It shows the Julia that install_library() would use (with its version, and whether it came from JULIA or the PATH), the library and what it was built from, each installed package that uses jlbind and whether the library is current for it, and the thread count. It works whether or not a library has loaded, and returns the same information invisibly as a list.
If the Julia installation used for the build has been removed or replaced, for example by a juliaup update, rebuild the library. install_library() rebuilds it when the Julia version differs from the one it was built with. If the version is the same, use force = TRUE:
jlbind::install_library(force = TRUE)
You can select the Julia installation to use by setting the JULIA environment variable or by passing julia = to install_library().
The library is compiled for the building machine’s CPU. To use it on other machines (e.g. cluster nodes), set JULIA_CPU_TARGET=generic and rebuild with force = TRUE.


Threads
Julia runs with one thread by default. To use multiple threads, set JULIA_NUM_THREADS before loading the first package that uses jlbind, for example in your .Renviron file:
JULIA_NUM_THREADS=auto # or a number, such as 4
The thread count is fixed when the library is loaded, so restart R after changing it.


Dependency versions
All clients share a single set of Julia dependencies. By default, the build starts from the versions in the Manifest.toml of the first client that has one, and keeps them for the other clients where their [compat] bounds allow. Pass versions = "compat" to ignore the manifests and let Julia’s resolver choose versions from the clients’ [compat] bounds alone.
If a client’s [compat] bounds conflict with those of the clients listed before it by jlbind_clients(), it is left out of the build; check_bound() says which clients it conflicts with.
You can control which clients are included by specifying them explicitly:
jlbind::install_library(packages = c("pkgA", "pkgC"))






ImportantClients with incompatible dependencies cannot share a library





If you need both clients but never need them in the same R session, build a separate library for each. Set JLBIND_LIBRARY before loading the client to select the library for that session.
For example, build the two libraries:
jlbind::build_library("pkgA", "~/jlbind/pkgA")
jlbind::build_library("pkgB", "~/jlbind/pkgB")
Then select one in an R session:
# jlbind.dll on Windows, jlbind.dylib on macOS
Sys.setenv(JLBIND_LIBRARY = "~/jlbind/pkgA/jlbind.so")
library(pkgA)

title: Get started with jlbind
text:
Source: vignettes/jlbind.qmd
jlbind lets an R package call Julia code without starting a separate Julia session. It compiles Julia code into a shared library using JuliaC.jl, then exposes Julia functions to R through native .Call() routines.
This vignette explains how to add Julia functions to your own R package with jlbind. An R package that uses jlbind is called a client. For how jlbind compares with other ways of calling Julia from R, see Performance.
An R process can load only one compiled Julia library1, so jlbind compiles the Julia code of all installed clients into one shared library, which each user builds with jlbind::install_library(). Your client therefore shares Julia dependency versions with every other client the user has installed. Using packages built on jlbind describes how this works and what your users need to do; your README should tell them to run jlbind::install_library() after installing your package.
For complete, working examples, see the two small clients that jlbind’s tests build: hellojl, which passes plain values, and counterjl, which keeps Julia objects in R (see Julia objects in R).

title: Get started with jlbind
text:
Set up
You need Julia 1.13 or later. From your R package’s directory, run:
jlbind::use_jlbind()
This creates the files and configuration needed to connect the package to jlbind:

inst/julia/, containing a Julia binding package named after the R package with a Bindings suffix (for example, MyPkgBindings), including an example function.
src/jlbind.c and src/entrypoints.h, which register the native routines, and a rule in src/Makevars that recompiles jlbind.c whenever entrypoints.h changes.
R/jlbind-wrappers.R, with an R function for each Julia function the binding package declares.
R/jlbind.R, which calls jlbind::bind_client() from .onLoad() and includes the roxygen tag for useDynLib().
The Config/jlbind, Imports: jlbind and SystemRequirements: Julia (>= 1.13) fields in DESCRIPTION.
A .jlbind/ directory for development builds, added to .Rbuildignore and .gitignore.

If your package already defines .onLoad(), add jlbind::bind_client(pkgname) to the existing function yourself. Then run devtools::document() to update NAMESPACE.






ImportantGive the Julia binding package a unique name



All clients are compiled into one library, so binding package names must be unique across all jlbind clients. The default, the R package name with a Bindings suffix, ensures this.

title: Get started with jlbind
text:
Declare Julia functions
Inside the binding package, declare each function that R should be able to call using @rcall. Each declaration specifies the argument types and return type expected by the binding.
For example:
module MyPkgBindings

using JLBind

greet(name::String) = "Hello, " * name * "!"
shift(x::Vector{Float64}, by::Union{Nothing,Float64}) =
    by === nothing ? x : x .+ by

@rcall greet(name::String)::String
@rcall shift(x::Vector{Float64}, by::Union{Nothing,Float64} = nothing)::Vector{Float64}

end
The binding package is an ordinary Julia package. Declare its dependencies in Project.toml and import them as usual.






ImportantWrite @rcall declarations literally at the top level



jlbind finds @rcall declarations by scanning the source files, not by running them, so write them literally at the top level of the module.

title: Get started with jlbind
text:
Call them from R
Whenever you add or change @rcall declarations, regenerate the native routine list:
jlbind::update_entrypoints()
This generates an R function for each declaration, in R/jlbind-wrappers.R:
greet <- function(name) .Call(C_greet, name)
shift <- function(x, by = NULL) .Call(C_shift, x, by)
Defaults in the declaration (literal numbers, strings, true, false or nothing) become R defaults.
To export or document a generated function, use a roxygen block on NULL with @name greet in another file. To add R code around a call, declare the Julia function with a jl_ prefix, e.g. @rcall jl_shift(...), and write shift() yourself.

title: Get started with jlbind
text:
Build and test locally
During development, you usually want to build the library from your package’s source rather than from the installed clients. Run:
jlbind::build_library()
devtools::load_all()
By default, build_library() writes the library to .jlbind/ in your package’s source directory. When you load the package with devtools::load_all(), jlbind uses this development library instead of the one created by install_library().
Once .jlbind/ exists, devtools::load_all() rebuilds it when your binding package’s files or your package’s version have changed since it was built.






NoteThe development library is only used when your package loads first



The .jlbind/ library is used only if your package is the first jlbind client loaded in the R session. A library that has loaded cannot be replaced, so after changing your Julia code, restart R; the next load_all() rebuilds it.


If you need to use a library stored elsewhere, set the JLBIND_LIBRARY environment variable to its path before loading the package.
You can also test against an unreleased version of a Julia dependency by providing a local checkout through develop:
jlbind::build_library(develop = "~/dev/SomePackage.jl")






TipPin the dependency versions



Include a Manifest.toml next to the binding package’s Project.toml with the Julia dependency versions known to compile with your package. CRAN’s policy asks that downloaded libraries be a fixed version rather than the latest.
The build uses the manifest of only the first client that has one (see Dependency versions), so keep your [compat] bounds accurate too.

title: Get started with jlbind
text:
Tests and CRAN
CRAN’s check machines do not have Julia installed, so your package must install and pass R CMD check without a compiled Julia library.
In tests, skip anything that needs the library:
skip_if_not(jlbind::is_bound("mypkg"))
In examples, wrap calls that require the library in if (jlbind::is_bound("mypkg")).
To check your package on GitHub Actions both ways, run:
jlbind::use_jlbind_ci()
This writes .github/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml, which runs R CMD check on Linux, Windows and macOS after compiling your package’s Julia code with build_library(), and once on Linux without Julia, as CRAN does.

title: Get started with jlbind
text:
Types
@rcall converts each argument using from_sexp() and converts the return value using to_sexp(). The built-in conversions are:
Single values








Julia
R argument
R result




String, Symbol
A single string
A character vector of length one


Float64
A single number
A double


Int64
A single whole number
A double


Int32
A single whole number
An integer


Int16, Int8, UInt16
A single whole number in range
An integer


UInt32
A single whole number in range
A double


Float32, Float16
A single number in range
A double


Bool
TRUE or FALSE
A logical


ComplexF64
A single complex number
A complex


Date
A single Date
A Date


DateTime
A single POSIXct
A POSIXct in UTC


Union{Missing,T}
A value of type T, or NA
A value of type T, or NA


Union{Nothing,T}
NULL, or a value of type T
NULL, or a value of type T


Nothing

NULL



Vectors and arrays








Julia
R argument
R result




Vector{String}, Vector{Symbol}
A character vector or factor
A character vector


Vector{Float64}, Vector{Int64}
A numeric vector
A double vector


Vector{Int32}

An integer vector


Vectors of the smaller types above
A numeric vector in range
An integer or double vector


Vector{Bool}

A logical vector


Vector{ComplexF64}
A complex or numeric vector
A complex vector


Vector{UInt8}
A raw vector
A raw vector


Vector{Date}
A Date vector
A Date vector


Vector{DateTime}
A POSIXct vector
A POSIXct vector in UTC


Vector{Union{Missing,T}}
A vector of type T, which can have NA
A vector of type T with NA


RVector{T}
A double, integer or raw vector
The same vector


Matrix{T}, Array{T,N}
A matrix or array of type T
A matrix or array of type T



Lists, data frames and references








Julia
R argument
R result




Other Vectors, Tuples
A list
A list


NamedTuple
A named list, such as a data frame
A named list


RDataFrame
A data frame
A data frame


Dict{String,T}, Dict{Symbol,T}
A named list
A named list, sorted by name


RRef{T}
A reference to a Julia object
A reference to a Julia object

A list of references



NA is an error unless the type is Union{Missing,T} or Vector{Union{Missing,T}}, which turn NA into missing and back. A number must fit its type, so an Int16 argument rejects 40000, and NaN is accepted only where missing is. Int64 results become doubles, since R’s integers have 32 bits; return Int32 for an R integer.
To use Date or DateTime, add the Dates standard library to the binding package’s dependencies.
A NamedTuple argument must have exactly the names of its fields, in any order, so you can pass a data frame as a named tuple of its columns. To take or return an actual data frame, wrap the columns in an RDataFrame. Its type lists the column names and the type of each column, so a type alias keeps signatures short:
const Sales = RDataFrame{(:group, :amount),Tuple{Vector{String},Vector{Float64}}}
const Summary = RDataFrame{(:group, :mean),Tuple{Vector{String},Vector{Float64}}}

function summarise(df::Sales)
    gs = sort(unique(df.group))
    means = [sum(df.amount[df.group .== g]) / count(==(g), df.group) for g in gs]
    return RDataFrame((group = gs, mean = means))
end

@rcall summarise(df::Sales)::Summary
summarise(data.frame(group = c("a", "b", "a"), amount = c(1, 2, 3)))
#>   group mean
#> 1     a    2
#> 2     b    2
An RDataFrame argument must be a data frame (a tibble works too) with exactly the declared columns, in any order, so select the columns in the R wrapper if the data frame has others: summarise(df[c("group", "amount")]). Its columns are its properties (df.group), and NamedTuple(df) returns them as a named tuple. Each column converts by the usual rules, so a factor column arrives as strings, and a Vector{Union{Missing,Float64}} column allows NA. Returning columns of different lengths is an error.
Errors inside a list name the element, as in element 2: expected a number.
Every other conversion copies, so a function given a large vector it only reads can take an RVector{Float64} (or RVector{Int32}, RVector{UInt8}). That is an AbstractVector viewing R’s memory, without checking for NA. It is valid only until the call returns, so don’t store it.
A binding package can support additional types by defining methods for JLBind.from_sexp(::Type{T}, x::SEXP) and JLBind.to_sexp(x::T). JLBind also provides helpers for building R objects directly, such as JLBind.data_frame() for a data frame whose columns are not known when the library is compiled. See the JLBind source for the existing conversions and helpers.

Julia objects in R
Sometimes an object is easier to keep in Julia than to convert into an R data structure. You can pass such objects by reference using RRef{T}. R receives an external pointer to the Julia object, allowing it to be reused across calls. The object is released when R garbage-collects the reference.
For example, define a mutable Julia object and expose functions that operate on it (the counterjl test client is a complete version of this):
mutable struct Counter
    n::Int64
end

JLBind.r_class(::Type{Counter}) = "counter"

new_counter(start::Int64) = Counter(start)
increment(c::Counter, by::Int64) = (c.n += by; c.n)

@rcall new_counter(start::Int64)::RRef{Counter}
@rcall increment(c::RRef{Counter}, by::Int64)::Int64
From R, you can create a counter and update it across calls:
counter <- new_counter(0)
class(counter)
#> [1] "counter"

increment(counter, 2)
#> [1] 2
r_class() sets the R class of the external pointer, so your package can define methods such as print() for it. An argument declared as RRef{Counter} also checks that the reference points to a Counter, rather than accepting an arbitrary Julia object.

title: Get started with jlbind
text:
Errors
If a function called through @rcall throws a Julia exception, jlbind turns it into an R error. The messages from ArgumentError, ErrorException, DimensionMismatch, OverflowError, and AssertionError are passed through. Other exceptions are summarized.

title: Get started with jlbind
text:
Compilation constraints (trimming)
By default, jlbind compiles the shared library with juliac --trim=safe. This keeps the compiled image small by including only code reachable from the functions exposed through @rcall. It also requires calls to be resolvable at compile time.
If your package cannot be compiled with trimming, add the following field to DESCRIPTION:
Config/jlbind/trim: false






Warning



An untrimmed library includes the full Julia system image and is much larger, so avoid it if you can.



Abstract types
With trimming, a common source of compilation errors is a function that accepts several concrete types through an abstract RRef. Suppose your binding package works with shapes:


Shape types and their areas

abstract type Shape end

struct Circle <: Shape
    radius::Float64
end
struct Square <: Shape
    side::Float64
end
struct Rectangle <: Shape
    width::Float64
    height::Float64
end
struct Triangle <: Shape
    base::Float64
    height::Float64
end

JLBind.r_class(::Type{<:Shape}) = "shape"

area(s::Circle) = pi * s.radius^2
area(s::Square) = s.side^2
area(s::Rectangle) = s.width * s.height
area(s::Triangle) = s.base * s.height / 2

An entrypoint that takes an RRef{Shape} knows only that its argument is some Shape. If it simply calls area(s), the compiler cannot tell which of the four methods that call reaches, and the build fails with an error such as:
Verifier error #1: unresolved call from statement area(s::Shape)::Any
One possible solution is to branch on the concrete types once, with @nospecialize, and to make the call inside each branch, where the type is known:
function with_shape(f::F, @nospecialize(s::Shape)) where {F}
    s isa Circle && return f(s)
    s isa Square && return f(s)
    s isa Rectangle && return f(s)
    s isa Triangle && return f(s)
    throw(ArgumentError("unknown shape"))
end

circle(radius::Float64) = Circle(radius)
square(side::Float64) = Square(side)
rectangle(width::Float64, height::Float64) = Rectangle(width, height)
triangle(base::Float64, height::Float64) = Triangle(base, height)
shape_area(@nospecialize(s::Shape)) = with_shape(area, s)
scaled_area(@nospecialize(s::Shape), factor::Float64) =
    with_shape(x -> factor^2 * area(x), s)

@rcall circle(radius::Float64)::RRef{Shape}
@rcall square(side::Float64)::RRef{Shape}
@rcall rectangle(width::Float64, height::Float64)::RRef{Shape}
@rcall triangle(base::Float64, height::Float64)::RRef{Shape}
@rcall shape_area(shape::RRef{Shape})::Float64
@rcall scaled_area(shape::RRef{Shape}, factor::Float64)::Float64
Every shape can then be passed to the same generated R functions:
shapes <- list(circle(1), square(2), rectangle(2, 3), triangle(2, 3))
vapply(shapes, shape_area, numeric(1))
#> [1] 3.141593 4.000000 6.000000 3.000000

scaled_area(square(2), 3)
#> [1] 36
Without @nospecialize, Julia compiles a separate with_shape for each concrete shape, and the call into it can’t be resolved, for the same reason as area(s). Functions that pass the shape on, such as shape_area, need it too (this small example happens to compile without it, since it is inlined).
If a hierarchy has only a few types, some alternatives to @nospecialize are:

Declare a separate entrypoint for each concrete type (RRef{Circle},RRef{Square}, …) and choose between them in R.
Use a small Union such as RRef{Union{Circle,Square}}, which Julia resolves by checking each member in turn.

title: Get started with jlbind
text:
Footnotes


JuliaC can privatize a library, giving it its own copy of the Julia runtime, but jlbind doesn’t use this. Each client would then ship a bundle with its own runtime and compiled copy of Base: about 60 MB per client on Linux and 100 MB on Windows, even for a tiny client, where a shared library adds only each client’s own code. Each runtime would also have its own garbage-collected heap and threads in memory, and Julia objects couldn’t be passed between clients. Privatization also doesn’t work on Windows yet (JuliaC.jl#151).↩︎

title: Performance
text:
Source: vignettes/articles/performance.qmd
jlbind calls Julia code that was compiled ahead of time, through one .Call() per function. The alternatives, JuliaCall and JuliaConnectoR, run Julia itself: JuliaCall embeds a Julia session in the R process, and JuliaConnectoR starts one in a separate process and talks to it over a socket. This article compares the three on the same Julia functions.
In short, on this machine, jlbind is ready to use 84 to 109 times sooner, and a call costs 0.702 µs rather than 8.76 µs (JuliaCall) or 207 µs (JuliaConnectoR).

title: Performance
text:
The benchmarks
The functions are those of benchjl, a minimal jlbind client kept next to the benchmark script:
greet(name::String) = "Hello, " * name * "!"
shift(x::Vector{Float64}, by::Float64) = x .+ by
jlbind calls them through benchjl, compiled into a jlbind library. JuliaCall and JuliaConnectoR evaluate the same definitions and call them with julia_call() and juliaFun(). Each interface runs in fresh R processes, since jlbind and JuliaCall can’t share one.

Startup: the time from loading the package to the result of the first call, greet("world"), in a new R process (R’s own startup excluded), repeated 10 times.
Call overhead: the median time of greet("world"), a string in and a string out, after the first call.
Data transfer: the median time of shift(x, 1) for numeric vectors x of length 10 to 107, which copies x to Julia and the result back.

The benchmark script is vignettes/articles/performance/benchmark.R. The results below were run on1:

For jlbind, startup is loading the compiled library and binding the package’s routines. JuliaCall and JuliaConnectoR start Julia, and compile each function the first time it is called. With a real Julia package instead of two one-line functions, compiling and loading the package typically take much longer than here.

A jlbind call is a .Call() into the compiled library, where the arguments are converted with R’s C API and the function is called directly. JuliaCall converts arguments and looks up the function at run time in the embedded session. JuliaConnectoR serializes the call to a separate Julia process and the result back, so each call costs a round trip.

Description
Lists the installed packages that install_library() will compile. A package uses jlbind if its DESCRIPTION has a Config/jlbind field. If a package is installed in more than one library, the copy that library() would load is the one listed.

Arguments



lib.loc


Library paths to search. Defaults to .libPaths().

title: List the packages that use jlbind
text:
Value
A data frame with one row per package and the columns package, version, module (the name of its Julia binding package), path (where the binding package is), trim (FALSE if it sets Config/jlbind/trim: false) and hash (a hash of the binding package’s files, which the library records to tell when it is out of date).

title: Build the Julia library
text: Source: R/library.R

title: Build the Julia library
text:
Description
Compiles the Julia code of every installed package that uses jlbind into one shared library, stored in tools::R_user_dir("jlbind", "data"). Run this after you install or update one of those packages. You need Julia 1.13 or later. The first build downloads and compiles the Julia dependencies, which can take a few minutes.

title: Build the Julia library
text:
Usage
install_library(
  packages = NULL,
  julia = NULL,
  ask = interactive(),
  force = FALSE,
  versions = c("manifest", "compat"),
  develop = NULL
)

title: Build the Julia library
text:
Arguments



packages


Names of the installed packages to build. By default, every package listed by jlbind_clients(). The others aren’t bound.




julia


Path to the julia executable. By default, the JULIA environment variable, or julia on the PATH.




ask


If TRUE, ask before building. Defaults to interactive().




force


If TRUE, rebuild even if the library is up to date. Always on with versions = "compat" or develop.




versions


Where the Julia dependency versions come from. "manifest" keeps the versions in the first package’s Manifest.toml where the other packages’ [compat] bounds allow. "compat" ignores the manifests and lets Julia’s resolver choose versions from the [compat] bounds alone.




develop


Paths to local Julia packages to use instead of their released versions.

title: Build the Julia library
text:
Details
All packages share one Julia environment. By default, the dependencies get the versions in the first package’s Manifest.toml. If two packages conflict, the one listed later by jlbind_clients() is left out, and check_bound() says why. See vignette("using-clients", "jlbind") for details.
The library is rebuilt only if it is out of date: built from other versions of the packages or other Julia code in them, by another version of jlbind or Julia, or with develop. If a library is already loaded, restart R to use the new one.

title: Build the Julia library
text:
Value
The path to the library (invisibly), or NULL if there was nothing to build.

title: Build the Julia library
text:
Examples
install_library()

# With a local checkout of a Julia dependency
install_library(develop = "~/dev/SomePackage.jl")

# Only two of the installed packages
install_library(packages = c("pkgA", "pkgB"))

Description
Writes a GitHub Actions workflow that checks the package with and without Julia. With Julia, it runs R CMD check on Linux, Windows and macOS after compiling the package’s Julia code with build_library(), so tests and examples that need the library run. Without Julia, it checks the package once on Linux, as CRAN does, where those tests and examples must be skipped. The workflow is written to .github/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml.

title: Report on the jlbind setup
text:
Description
Prints a report to run when a package that uses jlbind doesn’t work. It shows the Julia that builds the library, the library that is loaded (or would be) and what it was built from, the installed packages that use jlbind and whether the library is current for each, and the Julia thread count. It also works before a library has loaded.

title: Report on the jlbind setup
text:
Usage
jlbind_sitrep(julia = NULL)

title: Report on the jlbind setup
text:
Arguments



julia


Path to the julia executable. By default, the JULIA environment variable, or julia on the PATH.

title: Report on the jlbind setup
text:
Value
Invisibly, a list with:


julia: a list with path (NA if Julia was not found), source ("argument", "JULIA" or "PATH"), version (NA if it could not be run) and ok (whether it is Julia 1.13 or later).


library: a list with path, how ("loaded", "failed to load", "JLBIND_LIBRARY" or "default"), exists, build (how it was built: the jlbind and Julia versions, when, and whether it is trimmed, or NULL), problems (why it should be rebuilt or cannot load; empty if none) and objects (how many Julia objects R holds references to, or NULL if no library is loaded).


clients: a data frame with one row per package that uses jlbind or that the library was built for, with the columns package, version (installed), built (the version in the library), status ("ok", "left out", "not in the library", "built for version <v>", "Julia code changed" or "not installed") and bound.


threads: a list with count (from JULIA_NUM_THREADS) and fixed (TRUE once a library is loaded, after which the count cannot change).

title: Report on the jlbind setup
text:
Examples

jlbind_sitrep()
#> ── Julia (for building the library)
#> ✔ Julia 1.13.2 at /usr/bin/julia (from PATH)
#> ── Library
#> ✖ /home/runner/.local/share/R/jlbind/library/jlbind.so (default)
#> ✖ it has not been built
#> ── Packages that use jlbind
#>   none installed
#> ── Threads
#>   1 Julia thread (JULIA_NUM_THREADS unset)
